prompt: **Problem 2.1.1.** Resolutions of a crossing: if you travel along a knot and reach a crossing on the upper strand, the **0-resolution** turns left onto the lower strand and the **1-resolution** turns right. The picture shows a diagram of the figure-8 knot with crossings labelled $A,B,C,D$. Resolve crossing $B$ with a $0$-resolution (draw the diagram) and identify the resulting knot or link.
answer: Hopf link

solutions.title: Resolve and read off the result
solutions.body:
Resolve $B$ by a $0$-resolution; the other three crossings stay as they are. The resulting 3-crossing diagram has **two** components: the new connection at $B$ splits the single curve into two closed curves, one of which meets the other only in two crossings that link them once, while the remaining third crossing is a kink (removable by a Type I move). Removing the kink leaves the standard 2-crossing diagram of two linked circles.

*Check with the bracket polynomial.* Computing $\langle D_B\rangle$ for this 3-crossing diagram by the state sum gives $A^{-7}+A=(-A^{-3})(-A^4-A^{-4})$ (or its mirror image $A^{7}+A^{-1}$, depending on the drawing conventions): exactly a factor $-A^{\mp3}$ (one Type I kink, Problem 2.5.1) times the bracket $-A^4-A^{-4}$ of the Hopf link found in Example 2.6. A trefoil diagram would give $A^{\pm7}-A^{\pm3}-A^{\mp5}$ and the unknot a power of $-A^3$, so neither is possible.

**Answer: the Hopf link** (two unknotted circles linked once).

prompt: **Problem 2.1.2.** Resolutions of a crossing: travelling along the upper strand into a crossing, the **0-resolution** turns left onto the lower strand, the **1-resolution** turns right. Start with the figure-8 knot diagram in the picture (crossings $A,B,C,D$). It is possible to resolve one of the crossings so that the resulting diagram is a trefoil. Which crossing can we resolve ($A,B,C$ or $D$) and with which resolution ($0$ or $1$)? Simply state an answer.
answer: Resolve $A$ or $B$ with the 1-resolution, or $C$ or $D$ with the 0-resolution (any one of these four works).

solutions.title: Result
solutions.body:
The two top crossings $A,B$ are of one kind and the two crossings $C,D$ of the other (the figure-8 diagram is alternating and its checkerboard colouring is the same at $A,B$ and at $C,D$). At $A$ and $B$ the 0-resolution gives a Hopf link (Problem 2.1.1), while the **1-resolution gives a trefoil**; at $C$ and $D$ it is the other way round, so the **0-resolution gives the trefoil**.

*Check.* Computing the state sum of the 3-crossing diagram obtained in each of these four cases gives $A^7-A^3-A^{-5}$ (or its mirror image), which is the bracket polynomial of the trefoil (Fact 2.7), and the other four resolutions give $A^{\pm7}+A^{\mp1}$ (Hopf link with a kink).

**Answer: $A$ or $B$ with a 1-resolution; $C$ or $D$ with a 0-resolution.**

prompt: **Problem 2.3.1.** For a link diagram $D$ the *bracket polynomial* $\langle D\rangle$ (a Laurent polynomial in $A$) is determined by: (BP1) $\langle\bigcirc\rangle=1$ for a single circle with no crossings; (BP2) $\langle D\sqcup\bigcirc\rangle=(-A^2-A^{-2})\langle D\rangle$ if a circle not meeting the rest is added; (BP3) $\langle D\rangle=A\langle D_0\rangle+A^{-1}\langle D_1\rangle$, where $D_0,D_1$ are the $0$- and $1$-resolutions of any one crossing of $D$. (Travelling along the upper strand into a crossing, the $0$-resolution turns left onto the lower strand and the $1$-resolution turns right.) For a diagram $D$ with crossings numbered $1,\dots,n$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n$, $D_\epsilon$ is the *smoothing* in which crossing $i$ is resolved by an $\epsilon_i$-resolution (it has no crossings). Let $s_0(\epsilon),s_1(\epsilon)$ be the numbers of $0$- and $1$-resolutions used, $o(\epsilon)$ the number of circles of $D_\epsilon$, and $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^{s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)}\langle D_\epsilon\rangle$. $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)$. Let $D$ be a link diagram with $n$ crossings. Show that $\langle D\rangle=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle$.
answer: Apply BP3 at every crossing in turn; the coefficient of $\langle D_\epsilon\rangle$ is $A^{s_0-s_1}$.

solutions.title: Induction on the number of crossings
solutions.body:
For $n=0$, $D=D_\epsilon$ (empty tuple) and the sum has the single term $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^0\langle D\rangle$.

For $n\ge1$ apply BP3 to crossing $n$: $\langle D\rangle=A\langle D^{(0)}\rangle+A^{-1}\langle D^{(1)}\rangle$, where $D^{(e)}$ has $n-1$ crossings. By induction $\langle D^{(e)}\rangle=\sum_{\epsilon'\in\{0,1\}^{n-1}}A^{s_0(\epsilon')-s_1(\epsilon')}\langle D_{(\epsilon',e)}\rangle$ (the smoothings of $D^{(e)}$ are exactly the smoothings of $D$ with $\epsilon_n=e$). Multiplying by $A$ if $e=0$ and by $A^{-1}$ if $e=1$ adds one to $s_0-s_1$, resp. subtracts one, so the coefficient of $\langle D_\epsilon\rangle$ is $A^{s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)}$. Hence $\langle D\rangle=\sum_\epsilon\langle D,\epsilon\rangle$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.3.2.** For a link diagram $D$ the *bracket polynomial* $\langle D\rangle$ (a Laurent polynomial in $A$) is determined by: (BP1) $\langle\bigcirc\rangle=1$ for a single circle with no crossings; (BP2) $\langle D\sqcup\bigcirc\rangle=(-A^2-A^{-2})\langle D\rangle$ if a circle not meeting the rest is added; (BP3) $\langle D\rangle=A\langle D_0\rangle+A^{-1}\langle D_1\rangle$, where $D_0,D_1$ are the $0$- and $1$-resolutions of any one crossing of $D$. (Travelling along the upper strand into a crossing, the $0$-resolution turns left onto the lower strand and the $1$-resolution turns right.) For a diagram $D$ with crossings numbered $1,\dots,n$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n$, $D_\epsilon$ is the *smoothing* in which crossing $i$ is resolved by an $\epsilon_i$-resolution (it has no crossings). Let $s_0(\epsilon),s_1(\epsilon)$ be the numbers of $0$- and $1$-resolutions used, $o(\epsilon)$ the number of circles of $D_\epsilon$, and $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^{s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)}\langle D_\epsilon\rangle$. $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)$. Let $D$ be a link diagram and $\epsilon$ a smoothing. Show that $\langle D_\epsilon\rangle=(-A^2-A^{-2})^{\,o(\epsilon)-1}$.
answer: $D_\epsilon$ is $o(\epsilon)$ disjoint circles; use BP2 repeatedly and BP1 once.

solutions.title: Peel off circles
solutions.body: $D_\epsilon$ has no crossings, so it is a union of $o(\epsilon)$ disjoint circles. Remove one circle at a time using BP2: each removal multiplies the bracket by $(-A^2-A^{-2})$; after $o(\epsilon)-1$ removals a single circle remains, whose bracket is $1$ by BP1. Hence $\langle D_\epsilon\rangle=(-A^2-A^{-2})^{o(\epsilon)-1}$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.3.3.** For a diagram $D$ with crossings numbered $1,\dots,n$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n$, $D_\epsilon$ is the *smoothing* in which crossing $i$ is resolved by an $\epsilon_i$-resolution (it has no crossings). Let $s_0(\epsilon),s_1(\epsilon)$ be the numbers of $0$- and $1$-resolutions used, $o(\epsilon)$ the number of circles of $D_\epsilon$, and $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^{s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)}\langle D_\epsilon\rangle$. $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)$. Show that if two smoothings $\epsilon,\epsilon'$ of a link diagram differ in exactly one resolution, then $o(\epsilon')=o(\epsilon)\pm1$.
answer: Changing one resolution is a band move on the smoothed curve: it merges two circles or splits one.

solutions.title: Local picture
solutions.body:
$D_\epsilon$ and $D_{\epsilon'}$ coincide outside a small disc around the crossing $c$ where they differ; inside the disc, $D_\epsilon$ contains two arcs $a,b$ and $D_{\epsilon'}$ reconnects the same four endpoints the other way (a band move across the disc).

* If $a,b$ lie on different circles of $D_\epsilon$, reconnecting merges these two circles into one: $o(\epsilon')=o(\epsilon)-1$.
* If $a,b$ lie on the same circle $C$, then since $C$ is a simple closed curve in the plane and the band lies on one side of $C$ (inside or outside), reconnecting cuts $C$ into two circles: $o(\epsilon')=o(\epsilon)+1$.

Other circles are unaffected. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.4.1.** For a link diagram $D$ the *bracket polynomial* $\langle D\rangle$ (a Laurent polynomial in $A$) is determined by: (BP1) $\langle\bigcirc\rangle=1$ for a single circle with no crossings; (BP2) $\langle D\sqcup\bigcirc\rangle=(-A^2-A^{-2})\langle D\rangle$ if a circle not meeting the rest is added; (BP3) $\langle D\rangle=A\langle D_0\rangle+A^{-1}\langle D_1\rangle$, where $D_0,D_1$ are the $0$- and $1$-resolutions of any one crossing of $D$. (Travelling along the upper strand into a crossing, the $0$-resolution turns left onto the lower strand and the $1$-resolution turns right.) Show that if link diagrams $D$ and $D'$ are related by one Type II Reidemeister move (picture: two strands crossing twice on the left, pulled apart on the right), then $\langle D\rangle=\langle D'\rangle$. (You may use Problem 2.3.1: $\langle D\rangle$ is the sum over all smoothings.)
answer: Resolve the two crossings: of the four terms, three cancel, the fourth is $\langle D'\rangle$.

solutions.title: State sum on the two crossings

prompt: **Problem 2.4.2.** For a link diagram $D$ the *bracket polynomial* $\langle D\rangle$ (a Laurent polynomial in $A$) is determined by: (BP1) $\langle\bigcirc\rangle=1$ for a single circle with no crossings; (BP2) $\langle D\sqcup\bigcirc\rangle=(-A^2-A^{-2})\langle D\rangle$ if a circle not meeting the rest is added; (BP3) $\langle D\rangle=A\langle D_0\rangle+A^{-1}\langle D_1\rangle$, where $D_0,D_1$ are the $0$- and $1$-resolutions of any one crossing of $D$. (Travelling along the upper strand into a crossing, the $0$-resolution turns left onto the lower strand and the $1$-resolution turns right.) Show that if link diagrams $D$ and $D'$ are related by one Type III Reidemeister move (picture: one strand slides across the crossing of the other two), then $\langle D\rangle=\langle D'\rangle$. You may use that the bracket polynomial is invariant under Type II moves (Problem 2.4.1) and under planar isotopy.
answer: Resolve only the crossing of the two upper strands in both diagrams and compare termwise.

solutions.title: Resolve one crossing
solutions.body:
Let $t$ (top), $m$ (middle), $b$ (bottom) be the three strands, with $t$ over $m$ over $b$; let $x$ be the crossing of $t$ and $m$. In $D$ the strand $b$ crosses the two lower legs of $t,m$ (SW and SE of $x$); in $D'$ it has been slid to the other side of $x$, crossing the two upper legs (NW and NE). In both diagrams $b$ passes *under* $t$ and $m$.

Apply BP3 at $x$ in both diagrams: $\langle D\rangle=A\langle D_{\alpha}\rangle+A^{-1}\langle D_{\beta}\rangle$ and likewise for $D'$. The two smoothings at $x$ are the **horizontal** one (joins NW–NE and SW–SE) and the **vertical** one (joins NW–SW and NE–SE); the same smoothing carries the same coefficient in $D$ and $D'$ since $x$ is the same crossing. It suffices to compare diagrams with the same smoothing.

* *Horizontal smoothing.* In $D$ the strand $b$ crosses the lower arc SW–SE twice, passing under it both times; one Type II move removes both crossings, and $b$ ends up passing through the gap between the lower and the upper arc. In $D'$ the strand $b$ crosses the upper arc NW–NE twice (under it), and one Type II move again moves $b$ into the gap between the arcs. The two results are the same diagram, so the brackets agree (Problem 2.4.1, applied once to each).
* *Vertical smoothing.* The arcs are NW–SW and NE–SE; $b$ crosses each of them once, under both. Sliding $b$ along the two arcs from the lower position to the upper position is a planar isotopy that does not change any crossing, so the bracket is the same.

Hence $\langle D\rangle=\langle D'\rangle$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.5.1.** For a link diagram $D$ the *bracket polynomial* $\langle D\rangle$ (a Laurent polynomial in $A$) is determined by: (BP1) $\langle\bigcirc\rangle=1$ for a single circle with no crossings; (BP2) $\langle D\sqcup\bigcirc\rangle=(-A^2-A^{-2})\langle D\rangle$ if a circle not meeting the rest is added; (BP3) $\langle D\rangle=A\langle D_0\rangle+A^{-1}\langle D_1\rangle$, where $D_0,D_1$ are the $0$- and $1$-resolutions of any one crossing of $D$. (Travelling along the upper strand into a crossing, the $0$-resolution turns left onto the lower strand and the $1$-resolution turns right.) Show that for the one-crossing kink pictured (a strand with a small loop, i.e. a Type I configuration), $\langle\text{kink}\rangle=-A^{-3}\langle\text{straight strand}\rangle$.
answer: One smoothing gives the straight strand, the other gives the straight strand plus a small circle.

solutions.title: Apply BP3 to the crossing
solutions.body:
Resolving the single crossing of the kink gives two diagrams: for the pictured kink the $0$-resolution gives the plain strand $S$, the $1$-resolution gives $S$ together with a small disjoint circle. Hence by BP3 and BP2
$$\langle\text{kink}\rangle=A\langle S\rangle+A^{-1}(-A^2-A^{-2})\langle S\rangle=(A-A-A^{-3})\langle S\rangle=-A^{-3}\langle S\rangle.\ \blacksquare$$
(For the mirror kink the roles of $0$ and $1$ are swapped, giving $A^{-1}\langle S\rangle+A(-A^2-A^{-2})\langle S\rangle=-A^{3}\langle S\rangle$.)

prompt: **Problem 2.6.1.** For an oriented link diagram, crossings are *positive* or *negative* as in the first picture, $n_\pm(D)$ is the number of positive/negative crossings and the *writhe* is $w(D)=n_+(D)-n_-(D)$. Show that for the oriented kink pictured (either orientation of the strand) the writhe drops by one when the kink is removed: $w(\text{kink})=w(\text{straight strand})-1$ (all other parts of the diagram unchanged).
answer: The kink's single crossing is negative, so it contributes $-1$; removing it changes nothing else.

solutions.title: Count crossings
solutions.body: In the pictured kink the only crossing is a **negative** crossing (compare with Figure 2.3(b); the sign of a crossing does not depend on the orientation of the strand when both strands are reversed, which is what reversing the orientation of the single strand does: Fact 2.17). So it contributes $-1$ to $w$. Removing the kink deletes this crossing and leaves every other crossing, with its orientation and sign, unchanged. Hence $w(\text{kink})=w(\text{straight})+(-1)$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.6.2.** For an oriented link diagram, crossings are *positive* or *negative* as in the first picture and $w(D)=n_+(D)-n_-(D)$ is the writhe. Show that the writhe is unchanged by a Type II Reidemeister move, for each of the four choices of orientations of the two strands pictured.
answer: The two crossings created by a Type II move have opposite signs.

solutions.title: Opposite signs
solutions.body: In the left-hand diagram a strand $a$ lies over the other strand $b$ at both crossings $L,R$. Orient $a$ and $b$ in any of the four ways. Put coordinates with $a$ going from SW through $L$ along the upper edge, through $R$ to SE, and $b$ from NW through $L$ along the lower edge to $R$ and NE. Directions (for the orientation "left to right" on both): at $L$, $a$ points NE and $b$ points SE; at $R$, $a$ points SE and $b$ points NE. The sign of a crossing is determined by the sign of the cross product (direction of over strand) $\times$ (direction of under strand): at $L$ it is $(1,1)\times(1,-1)=-2<0$, at $R$ it is $(1,-1)\times(1,1)=+2>0$. Reversing the orientation of either strand multiplies the cross product at **both** crossings by $-1$, so the two crossings always have opposite signs. Hence the pair contributes $+1-1=0$ to the writhe, and the right-hand diagram (with no crossings there) has the same writhe. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.7.1.** For a link diagram $D$ the *bracket polynomial* $\langle D\rangle$ (a Laurent polynomial in $A$) is determined by: (BP1) $\langle\bigcirc\rangle=1$ for a single circle with no crossings; (BP2) $\langle D\sqcup\bigcirc\rangle=(-A^2-A^{-2})\langle D\rangle$ if a circle not meeting the rest is added; (BP3) $\langle D\rangle=A\langle D_0\rangle+A^{-1}\langle D_1\rangle$, where $D_0,D_1$ are the $0$- and $1$-resolutions of any one crossing of $D$. (Travelling along the upper strand into a crossing, the $0$-resolution turns left onto the lower strand and the $1$-resolution turns right.) Reidemeister moves (types I, II, III) change a diagram without changing the link; any two diagrams of the same link are connected by finitely many such moves. The *writhe* $w(D)=n_+(D)-n_-(D)$ of an oriented diagram is unchanged by Type II and III moves, and a Type I move changes it by $\mp1$ for the two kinds of kink; for the kink of Problem 2.5.1 (see the picture of the Type I move) the bracket satisfies $\langle\text{kink}\rangle=-A^{-3}\langle\text{straight}\rangle$ and $w(\text{kink})=w(\text{straight})-1$. Using also that the bracket polynomial is invariant under Type II and III moves, show that for an oriented link $L$ with diagram $D$ the polynomial $(-A)^{-3w(D)}\langle D\rangle$ is an invariant of $L$.
answer: Check invariance under each Reidemeister move; the factor $(-A)^{-3w}$ exactly compensates the factor $-A^{\mp3}$ from Type I moves.

solutions.title: Check the three moves
solutions.body:
By Reidemeister's theorem it suffices to show that $F(D)=(-A)^{-3w(D)}\langle D\rangle$ is unchanged by each Reidemeister move (applied to oriented diagrams).

* **Type II and III.** $\langle D\rangle$ is unchanged (Problems 2.4.1, 2.4.2) and $w(D)$ is unchanged (Problem 2.6.2 for Type II, Fact 2.19 for Type III). So $F$ is unchanged.
* **Type I, kink with a negative crossing** (Problem 2.5.1): $\langle D\rangle=-A^{-3}\langle D'\rangle$ and $w(D)=w(D')-1$, where $D'$ is the diagram with the kink removed. Since $-A^{-3}=(-A)^{-3}$,
$$F(D)=(-A)^{-3w(D')+3}(-A)^{-3}\langle D'\rangle=(-A)^{-3w(D')}\langle D'\rangle=F(D').$$
* **Type I, kink with a positive crossing.** Swapping the roles of the $0$- and $1$-resolutions as noted in Problem 2.5.1 gives $\langle D\rangle=-A^{3}\langle D'\rangle=(-A)^3\langle D'\rangle$ and $w(D)=w(D')+1$, so $F(D)=(-A)^{-3w(D')-3}(-A)^3\langle D'\rangle=F(D')$.

Thus $F$ does not change under any Reidemeister move, so it is an invariant of the oriented link. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.1.1.** For a link diagram $D$ the *bracket polynomial* $\langle D\rangle$ (a Laurent polynomial in $A$) is determined by: (BP1) $\langle\bigcirc\rangle=1$ for a single circle with no crossings; (BP2) $\langle D\sqcup\bigcirc\rangle=(-A^2-A^{-2})\langle D\rangle$ if a circle not meeting the rest is added; (BP3) $\langle D\rangle=A\langle D_0\rangle+A^{-1}\langle D_1\rangle$, where $D_0,D_1$ are the $0$- and $1$-resolutions of any one crossing of $D$. (Travelling along the upper strand into a crossing, the $0$-resolution turns left onto the lower strand and the $1$-resolution turns right.) For a diagram $D$ with crossings numbered $1,\dots,n$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n$, $D_\epsilon$ is the *smoothing* in which crossing $i$ is resolved by an $\epsilon_i$-resolution (it has no crossings). Let $s_0(\epsilon),s_1(\epsilon)$ be the numbers of $0$- and $1$-resolutions used, $o(\epsilon)$ the number of circles of $D_\epsilon$, and $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^{s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)}\langle D_\epsilon\rangle$. $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)$. For an oriented link diagram $D$ with writhe $w(D)$, the *Jones polynomial* of the link is $V(t)=(-A)^{-3w(D)}\langle D\rangle$ evaluated at $A=t^{-1/4}$ (it is a link invariant). Let $K^{\rm flip}$ be the mirror image of a knot $K$ (a diagram of $K^{\rm flip}$ is obtained from a diagram $D$ of $K$ by switching every crossing). Show that for every knot $K$, $V_{K^{\rm flip}}(t)=V_K(t^{-1})$.
answer: Switching all crossings swaps $0$- and $1$-resolutions, so $\langle D^{\rm flip}\rangle(A)=\langle D\rangle(A^{-1})$, and it negates the writhe.

solutions.title: Mirror image and the state sum
solutions.body:
Let $D$ be a diagram of $K$ with $n$ crossings and $D^{\rm flip}$ the diagram with every crossing switched (a diagram of $K^{\rm flip}$).

**Smoothings correspond.** At a crossing, switching over/under exchanges "left" and "right" in the rule defining the resolutions, so the $0$-resolution of the switched crossing is the $1$-resolution of the original one, and vice versa. Hence for $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n$ and the *dual* tuple $\hat\epsilon$ (every entry changed), $(D^{\rm flip})_{\hat\epsilon}=D_\epsilon$ as pictures. In particular $o(\hat\epsilon)=o(\epsilon)$ (for $D^{\rm flip}$), $s_0(\hat\epsilon)=s_1(\epsilon)$ and $s_1(\hat\epsilon)=s_0(\epsilon)$.

**Brackets.** By Problem 2.3.1–2.3.2, $\langle D\rangle(A)=\sum_\epsilon A^{s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{o(\epsilon)-1}$. The factor $(-A^2-A^{-2})^{o-1}$ is unchanged under $A\to A^{-1}$. Therefore
$$\langle D^{\rm flip}\rangle(A)=\sum_{\epsilon'}A^{s_0(\epsilon')-s_1(\epsilon')}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{o(\epsilon')-1}=\sum_\epsilon A^{-(s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon))}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{o(\epsilon)-1}=\langle D\rangle(A^{-1}),$$
where $\epsilon'=\hat\epsilon$ ranges over all tuples.

**Writhe.** Switching a crossing changes its sign (keeping the orientation), so $w(D^{\rm flip})=-w(D)$.

**Conclusion.** With $F_D(A)=(-A)^{-3w(D)}\langle D\rangle(A)$ we get
$$F_{D^{\rm flip}}(A)=(-A)^{3w(D)}\langle D\rangle(A^{-1})=\bigl((-A^{-1})^{-3w(D)}\langle D\rangle(A^{-1})\bigr)=F_D(A^{-1}).$$
Setting $A=t^{-1/4}$, $A^{-1}=t^{1/4}$ corresponds to replacing $t$ by $t^{-1}$, so $V_{K^{\rm flip}}(t)=V_K(t^{-1})$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.1.2.** A knot $K$ is *amphichiral* if it is equivalent to its mirror image $K^{\rm flip}$, and *chiral* otherwise. For the trefoil $K$ of the picture (Figure 3.1a) the Jones polynomial is $V_K(t)=-t^{-4}+t^{-3}+t^{-1}$, and $V_{K^{\rm flip}}(t)=V_K(t^{-1})$ for every knot. Is the trefoil amphichiral or chiral? Justify your answer.
answer: chiral

solutions.title: Compare Jones polynomials
solutions.body: By Problem 3.1.1, $V_{K^{\rm flip}}(t)=V_K(t^{-1})=-t^{4}+t^{3}+t$, which is different from $V_K(t)=-t^{-4}+t^{-3}+t^{-1}$ (different exponents). The Jones polynomial is a knot invariant, so equivalent knots have equal Jones polynomials. Hence $K\not\simeq K^{\rm flip}$: the trefoil is **chiral**. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.1.1.** The *crossing number* $c(K)$ of a knot $K$ is the minimum number of crossings in a diagram of $K$. The diagram in the picture (Figure 4.1) has seven crossings. Show that the crossing number of that knot is not $7$.
answer: Rotate one half of the diagram by $180^\circ$ about the horizontal axis: this undoes the middle crossing and keeps the other crossings, giving a 6-crossing diagram.

solutions.title: Flip one half
solutions.body: The diagram consists of two clasps of three crossings each, joined through a single middle crossing (the two connecting strands cross once). Rotate the right-hand clasp by $180^\circ$ about the horizontal axis through the middle of the picture (a rigid motion of that part of the knot in space, holding the two connecting strands' endpoints). The two connecting strands, which formed the middle crossing, are untwisted by this rotation, so that crossing disappears; the three crossings inside the rotated clasp are carried to three crossings (the rotation only reflects the clasp's diagram vertically and exchanges over and under, preserving the number of crossings). The result is a diagram of the same knot with $3+3=6$ crossings. Hence $c(K)\le6<7$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.2.1.** A knot diagram $D$ is *un-reduced* if it has the form of the picture (Figure 4.2: in the region between the parts $X$ and $Y$ there are exactly two strands going from $X$ to $Y$, and these two strands cross each other exactly once); otherwise it is *reduced*. Show, by drawing an example, that two diagrams $D,D'$ of the same knot $K$ can exist with $D$ reduced and $D'$ having fewer crossings than $D$.
answer: Take the unknot: the plain circle versus a reduced 3-crossing diagram (a trefoil projection with one crossing switched).

solutions.title: Unknot example
solutions.body:
Let $D'$ be the usual circle (the unknot with $0$ crossings). Let $D$ be the standard three-crossing projection of the trefoil, but with crossing $b$ switched so that, traversing the curve from a suitable base point, the six passages through crossings are over, over, over, under, under, under (in the order $a,b,c,a,b,c$ of the crossings). In the alternating trefoil the passages are over, under, over, under, over, under, so switching $b$ (both of its passages) gives exactly this pattern.

* $D$ is a diagram of the **unknot**: it is *descending* (from the base point every crossing is first met as an over-crossing), so we can lift the curve to continuously decreasing height and then it is clearly unknotted.
* $D$ is **reduced**: being reduced depends only on the projection (which crossings/strands exist), and in the trefoil projection no crossing has the form of Figure 4.2 (removing any one crossing leaves a connected curve; cutting the plane along a loop through any single crossing and meeting nothing else is impossible, since every face of this projection has at least two crossings on its boundary).

So $D$ and $D'$ are both diagrams of the unknot, $D$ is reduced with 3 crossings, and $D'$ has $0$ crossings. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.3.1.** The diagram of a knot determines a planar graph: its vertices are the crossings, its edges are the arcs between consecutive crossings. Euler's formula says $V-E+F=2$ for a connected planar graph with $V$ vertices, $E$ edges and $F$ faces (the outside counts as a face). Show that the graph of a knot diagram with $n$ crossings has $n+2$ faces.
answer: $V=n$, every vertex has degree 4 so $E=2n$, and Euler gives $F=n+2$.

solutions.title: Euler's formula
solutions.body:
A knot diagram is a single closed curve, so its graph is connected. If $n=0$ the diagram is a circle with two faces (inside and outside), $=n+2$.
For $n\ge1$: $V=n$, and each crossing involves exactly two strands, so every vertex has degree $4$. Counting pairs (edge, endpoint) in two ways, $2E=4V$, so $E=2n$. Euler's formula gives $F=2-V+E=2-n+2n=n+2$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.4.1.** Colour the faces of a knot diagram in a checkerboard pattern (adjacent faces get different colours; the outside is a face). At a crossing, the four wedges are coloured as in one of the two pictures: the colouring is *0-separating* if the black wedges are the ones that the $0$-resolution separates (first picture), and *1-separating* otherwise. (Travelling along the upper strand into a crossing, the $0$-resolution turns left onto the lower strand, the $1$-resolution turns right.) A knot diagram is *alternating* if its strand goes alternately over and under at successive crossings. Show that a knot diagram is alternating if and only if it admits a checkerboard colouring in which every crossing is 0-separating.
answer: Follow the strand: the shaded side stays constant along an edge; a 0-separating crossing switches it from left to right on the over-strand and from right to left on the under-strand.

solutions.title: Track the shaded side along the strand
solutions.body:
Orient the knot and travel along it. Along an edge between consecutive crossings the shaded face is always on the same side (left or right) of the strand, since the edge borders one shaded and one unshaded face. Rotate a crossing so that the over strand is "/" (SW–NE). Then a crossing is 0-separating iff the black wedges are W and E (the $0$-resolution turns left from the over strand, joining SW with NW and NE with SE, and so separates W from E).

*Behaviour at a crossing.* Heading NE along the over strand: before the crossing the wedges beside the strand are W (left) and S (right); after it, N (left) and E (right). Heading SE along the under strand: before, N (left) and W (right); after, S (right) and E (left). Hence:

* *0-separating* (W,E black): over strand: shaded side left before, right after; under strand: right before, left after.
* *1-separating* (N,S black): over strand: right before, left after; under strand: left before, right after.

(For the 1-separating case, over: before S (right), after N (left); under: before N (left), after S (right).)

**($\Leftarrow$)** Suppose all crossings are 0-separating. The shaded side after a crossing equals the shaded side before the next one. If we leave an over-crossing, the shaded side is right; the next crossing (0-separating) with shaded side right before it is an *under* crossing (0-sep. over needs left before), and we leave it with shaded side left, so the next one is over, and so on. The strand alternates over/under: the diagram is alternating.

**($\Rightarrow$)** Suppose the diagram is alternating. Colour the faces in a checkerboard way; if some crossing $C$ is 1-separating, swap all colours (this changes every crossing's type), so we may assume $C$ is 0-separating. Say we leave $C$ as an over strand: the shaded side is right. The next crossing is under (alternating), met with shaded side right before it; by the table only a 0-separating crossing is entered on the right when passing under, so it is 0-separating and we leave it with shaded side left. The next crossing is over, entered with shaded side left: again only a 0-separating crossing allows this. By induction, all crossings along the knot (which passes through every crossing) are 0-separating. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.5.1.** For a link diagram $D$ the *bracket polynomial* $\langle D\rangle$ (a Laurent polynomial in $A$) is determined by: (BP1) $\langle\bigcirc\rangle=1$ for a single circle with no crossings; (BP2) $\langle D\sqcup\bigcirc\rangle=(-A^2-A^{-2})\langle D\rangle$ if a circle not meeting the rest is added; (BP3) $\langle D\rangle=A\langle D_0\rangle+A^{-1}\langle D_1\rangle$, where $D_0,D_1$ are the $0$- and $1$-resolutions of any one crossing of $D$. (Travelling along the upper strand into a crossing, the $0$-resolution turns left onto the lower strand and the $1$-resolution turns right.) Reidemeister moves (types I, II, III) change a diagram without changing the link; any two diagrams of the same link are connected by finitely many such moves. For a Laurent polynomial $f$ let $\mathrm{hp}(f)$ and $\mathrm{lp}(f)$ be its highest and lowest exponents and $\mathrm{span}(f)=\mathrm{hp}(f)-\mathrm{lp}(f)$. The bracket polynomial is invariant under Type II and III moves, and a Type I move multiplies it by $(-A)^{\pm3}$ (Problem 2.5.1). Let $D_1,D_2$ be diagrams of the same knot. Show that $\mathrm{span}\langle D_1\rangle=\mathrm{span}\langle D_2\rangle$.
answer: The diagrams differ by Reidemeister moves; Types II/III keep $\langle D\rangle$, Type I multiplies it by $\pm A^{\pm3}$, which does not change the span.

solutions.title: Reidemeister moves
solutions.body: By Reidemeister's theorem $D_1$ is carried to $D_2$ by finitely many Reidemeister moves. Types II and III do not change $\langle D\rangle$ (Problems 2.4.1, 2.4.2); a Type I move multiplies $\langle D\rangle$ by $-A^{3}$ or $-A^{-3}$ (Problem 2.5.1 and its mirror), which shifts all exponents by $\pm3$ and so leaves $\mathrm{hp}-\mathrm{lp}$ unchanged. Hence the span is unchanged along the sequence. $\blacksquare$

solutions.title: Via the Jones polynomial
solutions.body: $V_K(t)=(-A)^{-3w(D)}\langle D\rangle$ at $A=t^{-1/4}$ is a knot invariant (Problem 2.7.1). The factor $(-A)^{-3w}$ only shifts exponents of $A$, so $\mathrm{span}_A\langle D\rangle=4\,\mathrm{span}_tV_K$ for any diagram $D$ of $K$; this depends only on $K$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.5.2.** For a diagram $D$ with crossings numbered $1,\dots,n$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n$, $D_\epsilon$ is the *smoothing* in which crossing $i$ is resolved by an $\epsilon_i$-resolution (it has no crossings). Let $s_0(\epsilon),s_1(\epsilon)$ be the numbers of $0$- and $1$-resolutions used, $o(\epsilon)$ the number of circles of $D_\epsilon$, and $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^{s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)}\langle D_\epsilon\rangle$. $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)$. Let $\mathrm{hp}$ denote the highest exponent of $A$. For a knot diagram $D$ and a smoothing $\epsilon$ show that $\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)+2o(\epsilon)-2$.
answer: $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^{s_0-s_1}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{o-1}$.

solutions.title: Leading term
solutions.body: By Problem 2.3.2, $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^{s_0-s_1}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{o-1}$. The polynomial $(-A^2-A^{-2})^{o-1}$ has highest term $(-1)^{o-1}A^{2(o-1)}$ (nonzero coefficient), so $\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=s_0-s_1+2(o-1)$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.5.3.** For a diagram $D$ with crossings numbered $1,\dots,n$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n$, $D_\epsilon$ is the *smoothing* in which crossing $i$ is resolved by an $\epsilon_i$-resolution (it has no crossings). Let $s_0(\epsilon),s_1(\epsilon)$ be the numbers of $0$- and $1$-resolutions used, $o(\epsilon)$ the number of circles of $D_\epsilon$, and $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^{s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)}\langle D_\epsilon\rangle$. $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)$. Using $\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)+2o(\epsilon)-2$ and the fact that changing one resolution changes $o$ by $\pm1$, show that for a knot diagram $D$, $\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\mathbf 0\rangle\ge\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle$ for all smoothings $\epsilon$.
answer: Changing a 0-resolution into a 1-resolution never raises $\mathrm{hp}$; reach any $\epsilon$ from $\mathbf 0$ by such changes.

solutions.title: Monotone path from $\mathbf 0$
solutions.body:
Let $\epsilon'$ be obtained from $\epsilon$ by changing one $0$-resolution into a $1$-resolution. Then $s_0-s_1$ decreases by $2$, and $o(\epsilon')=o(\epsilon)\pm1$ (Problem 2.3.3), so $2o$ changes by $\pm2$. Hence
$$\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\epsilon'\rangle=\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle-2\pm2\le\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle.$$
Given any $\epsilon$, start at $\mathbf 0$ and change, one at a time, the $0$'s at the positions where $\epsilon$ has a $1$; $\mathrm{hp}$ never increases along the way, so $\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle\le\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\mathbf 0\rangle$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.5.4.** For a diagram $D$ with crossings numbered $1,\dots,n$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n$, $D_\epsilon$ is the *smoothing* in which crossing $i$ is resolved by an $\epsilon_i$-resolution (it has no crossings). Let $s_0(\epsilon),s_1(\epsilon)$ be the numbers of $0$- and $1$-resolutions used, $o(\epsilon)$ the number of circles of $D_\epsilon$, and $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^{s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)}\langle D_\epsilon\rangle$. $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)$. Let $D$ be a knot diagram with $n$ crossings. Using $\langle D\rangle=\sum_\epsilon\langle D,\epsilon\rangle$ and $\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\mathbf 0\rangle\ge\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle$ for all $\epsilon$, show that $\mathrm{hp}\langle D\rangle\le n+2o(\mathbf 0)-2$.
answer: The highest power of a sum is at most the maximum; at $\mathbf 0$, $s_0-s_1=n$.

solutions.title: Bound the sum
solutions.body: $\mathrm{hp}\langle D\rangle\le\max_\epsilon\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\mathbf 0\rangle=n+2o(\mathbf 0)-2$, since for $\epsilon=\mathbf 0$ we have $s_0=n$, $s_1=0$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.5.5.** For a diagram $D$ with crossings numbered $1,\dots,n$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n$, $D_\epsilon$ is the *smoothing* in which crossing $i$ is resolved by an $\epsilon_i$-resolution (it has no crossings). Let $s_0(\epsilon),s_1(\epsilon)$ be the numbers of $0$- and $1$-resolutions used, $o(\epsilon)$ the number of circles of $D_\epsilon$, and $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^{s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)}\langle D_\epsilon\rangle$. $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)$. Let $D$ be a knot diagram with $n$ crossings, and assume $\mathrm{hp}\langle D\rangle\le n+2o(\mathbf 0)-2$. Show that $\mathrm{span}\langle D\rangle\le2n+2\bigl(o(\mathbf 0)+o(\mathbf 1)\bigr)-4$.
answer: Mirror argument for the lowest power: $\mathrm{lp}\langle D\rangle\ge-n-2o(\mathbf 1)+2$.

solutions.title: Lowest power
solutions.body:
By the same computation as 4.5.2, $\mathrm{lp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=s_0-s_1-2o+2$. Changing a $0$-resolution into a $1$-resolution changes $s_0-s_1$ by $-2$ and $-2o$ by $\mp2$, so $\mathrm{lp}$ changes by $-2\mp2\le0$: $\mathrm{lp}$ never increases when we move from $\epsilon$ towards $\mathbf 1$ one flip at a time. Therefore $\mathrm{lp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle\ge\mathrm{lp}\langle D,\mathbf 1\rangle=-n-2o(\mathbf 1)+2$ for all $\epsilon$, and so $\mathrm{lp}\langle D\rangle\ge-n-2o(\mathbf 1)+2$. Subtracting from the bound on $\mathrm{hp}\langle D\rangle$:
$$\mathrm{span}\langle D\rangle\le(n+2o(\mathbf 0)-2)-(-n-2o(\mathbf 1)+2)=2n+2(o(\mathbf 0)+o(\mathbf 1))-4.\ \blacksquare$$

prompt: **Problem 4.6.1.** For a diagram $D$ with crossings numbered $1,\dots,n$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n$, $D_\epsilon$ is the *smoothing* in which crossing $i$ is resolved by an $\epsilon_i$-resolution (it has no crossings). Let $s_0(\epsilon),s_1(\epsilon)$ be the numbers of $0$- and $1$-resolutions used, $o(\epsilon)$ the number of circles of $D_\epsilon$, and $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^{s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)}\langle D_\epsilon\rangle$. $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)$. A link diagram is *connected* if its graph is connected (a knot diagram always is). Let $D$ be a connected link diagram with $n$ crossings. Show that $o(\mathbf 0)+o(\mathbf 1)\le n+2$. (You may use Problem 2.3.3.)
answer: Induct on $n$: resolving one crossing keeps the diagram connected for at least one choice of resolution; compare the all-0/all-1 states.

solutions.title: Induction on $n$
solutions.body:
**Base $n=0$.** A connected diagram with no crossings is one circle, so $o(\mathbf 0)=o(\mathbf 1)=1$ and $2\le0+2$.

**Step.** Let $D$ be connected with $n+1\ge1$ crossings and let $x$ be a crossing.

*Claim: at least one of the two resolutions of $x$ leaves a connected diagram.* Let $h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4$ be the half-edges at $x$ in cyclic order; the $0$-resolution pairs $(h_1h_2),(h_3h_4)$, the $1$-resolution pairs $(h_2h_3),(h_4h_1)$. Remove $x$; call a *piece* each connected component of the rest of the graph (and each edge that is a loop at $x$, joining two of the $h_i$). Every piece is attached to $x$ by an even number $\ge2$ of half-edges: for a component with $V'$ vertices, all of degree 4 except for the attachments, the degree sum is $4V'-k$, which must be even, so $k$ is even (and $k\ge1$ by connectivity of $D$). The resolved diagram is connected iff the pieces, joined through the pairs of half-edges, form one block. If *both* resolutions left a disconnected diagram, every piece would have all its attachments inside one pair of $\{h_1h_2|h_3h_4\}$ and inside one pair of $\{h_2h_3|h_4h_1\}$, so every piece would be attached by a single half-edge, contradicting that $k$ is even. This proves the claim.

Say (by symmetry) the $0$-resolution at $x$ gives a connected diagram $E$ with $n$ crossings. The smoothings of $E$ are smoothings of $D$ with $\epsilon_x=0$: $E_{\mathbf 0}=D_{\mathbf 0}$, and $E_{\mathbf 1}$ is the smoothing of $D$ that differs from $D_{\mathbf 1}$ exactly at $x$, so $o(E_{\mathbf 1})=o(D_{\mathbf 1})\pm1$ by Problem 2.3.3. By the induction hypothesis $o(E_{\mathbf 0})+o(E_{\mathbf 1})\le n+2$, hence
$$o(D_{\mathbf 0})+o(D_{\mathbf 1})\le o(E_{\mathbf 0})+o(E_{\mathbf 1})+1\le n+3=(n+1)+2.\ \blacksquare$$

prompt: **Problem 4.6.2.** Let $D$ be a knot diagram with $n$ crossings. Using $\mathrm{span}\langle D\rangle\le2n+2(o(\mathbf 0)+o(\mathbf 1))-4$ and $o(\mathbf 0)+o(\mathbf 1)\le n+2$ for connected diagrams, show that $\mathrm{span}\langle D\rangle\le4n$.
answer: Substitute $o(\mathbf 0)+o(\mathbf 1)\le n+2$.

solutions.title: Combine
solutions.body: A knot diagram is connected, so $o(\mathbf 0)+o(\mathbf 1)\le n+2$ and $\mathrm{span}\langle D\rangle\le2n+2(n+2)-4=4n$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.7.1.** For a diagram $D$ with crossings numbered $1,\dots,n$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n$, $D_\epsilon$ is the *smoothing* in which crossing $i$ is resolved by an $\epsilon_i$-resolution (it has no crossings). Let $s_0(\epsilon),s_1(\epsilon)$ be the numbers of $0$- and $1$-resolutions used, $o(\epsilon)$ the number of circles of $D_\epsilon$, and $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^{s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)}\langle D_\epsilon\rangle$. $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)$. A knot diagram is *alternating* if its strand alternates between over and under at successive crossings, and *reduced* if it is not of the pictured form (Figure 4.2: a part $X$ and a part $Y$ joined by exactly two strands that cross each other exactly once; i.e. no crossing is 'nugatory'). You may use: an alternating diagram admits a checkerboard colouring in which every crossing is 0-separating (the $0$-resolution separates the two black wedges). Show that if $D$ is a reduced alternating diagram and $\epsilon$ is a smoothing with exactly one $1$-resolution, then $o(\mathbf 0)=o(\epsilon)+1$.
answer: Circles of $D_{\mathbf 0}$ are the boundaries of the black faces; the single $1$-resolution joins two black faces, which are different because $D$ is reduced.

solutions.title: Black faces and bridges
solutions.body:
Colour $D$ as in the hint (all crossings 0-separating). At each crossing the $0$-resolution cuts the two black wedges apart and merges the two white wedges. Hence the circles of $D_{\mathbf 0}$ are exactly the boundaries of the black faces (follow the boundary of a black face: at each corner the smoothing arc hugs the black wedge), so $o(\mathbf 0)$ is the number of black faces.

Now let $\epsilon$ have a single $1$ at crossing $c$. Changing the $0$-resolution at $c$ to a $1$-resolution adds a "bridge" joining the two black wedges at $c$. If these two wedges belong to different black faces $F,F'$, the circles bounding $F$ and $F'$ merge into one circle and no other circle changes, so $o(\epsilon)=o(\mathbf 0)-1$.

They cannot belong to the same black face: otherwise there is a simple closed curve $\gamma$ through $c$ lying in that face away from $c$ (entering from one black wedge and leaving through the other), meeting the diagram only at $c$. $\gamma$ separates the plane into an inside and an outside, with the legs NW,NE of $c$ on one side and SW,SE on the other; so the diagram consists of a part $X$ outside and a part $Y$ inside joined by exactly the two strands through $c$, which cross once there — the form of Figure 4.2, contradicting that $D$ is reduced. Hence $o(\mathbf 0)=o(\epsilon)+1$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.7.2.** For a diagram $D$ with crossings numbered $1,\dots,n$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n$, $D_\epsilon$ is the *smoothing* in which crossing $i$ is resolved by an $\epsilon_i$-resolution (it has no crossings). Let $s_0(\epsilon),s_1(\epsilon)$ be the numbers of $0$- and $1$-resolutions used, $o(\epsilon)$ the number of circles of $D_\epsilon$, and $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^{s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)}\langle D_\epsilon\rangle$. $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)$. Show that the assumption that $D$ is reduced is needed in the statement 'if $D$ is a reduced alternating diagram and $\epsilon$ is a smoothing with exactly one $1$-resolution then $o(\mathbf 0)=o(\epsilon)+1$': give an example where $D$ is alternating (but not reduced) and $o(\mathbf 0)\ne o(\epsilon)+1$ for some $\epsilon$ with exactly one $1$-resolution.
answer: A one-crossing diagram of the unknot (a figure-eight shaped curve) with the crossing chosen so that its $0$-resolution gives a single circle.

solutions.title: One-crossing kink
solutions.body: Take the figure-eight-shaped curve with one crossing (a diagram of the unknot) and draw the crossing so that its $0$-resolution is the one that keeps a single circle (the other choice of over/under swaps $0$ and $1$). With one crossing the diagram is trivially alternating, and it is not reduced (the crossing is of the form in Figure 4.2: the two lobes are joined only through that crossing). Take $\epsilon=(1)$. Then $D_{\mathbf 0}$ is one circle and $D_\epsilon$ splits off a small circle, so $o(\mathbf 0)=1$ but $o(\epsilon)+1=3$. Hence $o(\mathbf 0)\ne o(\epsilon)+1$, while for the other drawing of the crossing $o(\mathbf 0)=2=o(\epsilon)+1$ holds. This shows that reducedness is needed (the black face containing both wedges at the crossing is the outside here). $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.7.3.** For a link diagram $D$ the *bracket polynomial* $\langle D\rangle$ (a Laurent polynomial in $A$) is determined by: (BP1) $\langle\bigcirc\rangle=1$ for a single circle with no crossings; (BP2) $\langle D\sqcup\bigcirc\rangle=(-A^2-A^{-2})\langle D\rangle$ if a circle not meeting the rest is added; (BP3) $\langle D\rangle=A\langle D_0\rangle+A^{-1}\langle D_1\rangle$, where $D_0,D_1$ are the $0$- and $1$-resolutions of any one crossing of $D$. (Travelling along the upper strand into a crossing, the $0$-resolution turns left onto the lower strand and the $1$-resolution turns right.) For a diagram $D$ with crossings numbered $1,\dots,n$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n$, $D_\epsilon$ is the *smoothing* in which crossing $i$ is resolved by an $\epsilon_i$-resolution (it has no crossings). Let $s_0(\epsilon),s_1(\epsilon)$ be the numbers of $0$- and $1$-resolutions used, $o(\epsilon)$ the number of circles of $D_\epsilon$, and $\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=A^{s_0(\epsilon)-s_1(\epsilon)}\langle D_\epsilon\rangle$. $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)$. You may use all earlier results of this problem set, in particular: (i) $\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=s_0-s_1+2o-2$ and $\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\mathbf 0\rangle\ge\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle$ for all $\epsilon$ (and the mirror statement for $\mathrm{lp}$); (ii) a knot diagram with $n$ crossings has a graph with $n+2$ faces; (iii) an alternating diagram has a checkerboard colouring with all crossings $0$-separating, and for a reduced alternating diagram, $o(\mathbf 0)=o(\epsilon)+1$ whenever $\epsilon$ has exactly one $1$-resolution. Let $D$ be a reduced alternating knot diagram with $n$ crossings. Show that $\mathrm{span}\langle D\rangle=4n$.
answer: Strict inequalities make the extreme terms $\langle D,\mathbf 0\rangle$ and $\langle D,\mathbf 1\rangle$ survive; then $o(\mathbf 0)+o(\mathbf 1)$ is the number of faces, $n+2$.

solutions.title: Extreme terms survive
solutions.body:
Colour $D$ checkerboard with all crossings $0$-separating. As in 4.7.1, the circles of $D_{\mathbf 0}$ are the boundaries of the black faces and the circles of $D_{\mathbf 1}$ are the boundaries of the white faces (at every crossing the $1$-resolution separates the two white wedges). Hence $o(\mathbf 0)+o(\mathbf 1)$ is the total number of faces $=n+2$ (Problem 4.3.1).

**Highest power.** Let $\epsilon\ne\mathbf 0$. Reach $\epsilon$ from $\mathbf 0$ by changing $0$'s into $1$'s one at a time, first changing one position to get $\epsilon_1$ with exactly one $1$. Along such a path $\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\cdot\rangle$ never increases (Problem 4.5.3), and the first step is strict: $o(\epsilon_1)=o(\mathbf 0)-1$ by 4.7.1, so
$$\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\epsilon_1\rangle=(n-2)+2(o(\mathbf 0)-1)-2=\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\mathbf 0\rangle-4.$$
Hence $\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle\le\mathrm{hp}\langle D,\mathbf 0\rangle-4$ for every $\epsilon\ne\mathbf 0$. In $\langle D\rangle=\langle D,\mathbf 0\rangle+\sum_{\epsilon\ne\mathbf 0}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle$ no cancellation of the top term is possible, so $\mathrm{hp}\langle D\rangle=n+2o(\mathbf 0)-2$.

**Lowest power.** By the same argument with the colours exchanged (circles of $D_{\mathbf 1}$ are boundaries of white faces; changing one $1$ to a $0$ at a crossing joins two white wedges, which lie in different white faces because $D$ is reduced), $o(\epsilon')=o(\mathbf 1)-1$ for $\epsilon'$ with exactly one $0$. Since $\mathrm{lp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle=s_0-s_1-2o+2$ is non-decreasing along flips $1\to0$ (Problem 4.5.5's argument reversed) and $\mathrm{lp}\langle D,\epsilon'\rangle=(-n+2)-2(o(\mathbf 1)-1)+2=\mathrm{lp}\langle D,\mathbf 1\rangle+4$, we get $\mathrm{lp}\langle D,\epsilon\rangle\ge\mathrm{lp}\langle D,\mathbf 1\rangle+4$ for $\epsilon\ne\mathbf 1$, so $\mathrm{lp}\langle D\rangle=-n-2o(\mathbf 1)+2$.

**Span.**
$$\mathrm{span}\langle D\rangle=(n+2o(\mathbf 0)-2)-(-n-2o(\mathbf 1)+2)=2n+2\bigl(o(\mathbf 0)+o(\mathbf 1)\bigr)-4=2n+2(n+2)-4=4n.\ \blacksquare$$

prompt: **Problem 4.8.1.** The *crossing number* $c(K)$ of a knot $K$ is the minimum number of crossings in a diagram of $K$, and $\mathrm{span}\,V_K$ is the span of its Jones polynomial in $t$. For every knot diagram $D$ with $n$ crossings, $\mathrm{span}\langle D\rangle\le4n$ and $V_K(t)=(-A)^{-3w(D)}\langle D\rangle$ at $A=t^{-1/4}$. Show that $c(K)\ge\mathrm{span}\,V_K$ for every knot $K$.
answer: Take a diagram with $c(K)$ crossings: $4\,\mathrm{span}\,V_K=\mathrm{span}\langle D\rangle\le4c(K)$.

solutions.title: Minimal diagram
solutions.body: Let $D$ be a diagram of $K$ with exactly $c(K)$ crossings. Multiplying by $(-A)^{-3w(D)}$ shifts the exponents of $A$, and $t=A^{-4}$, so $\mathrm{span}_tV_K=\tfrac14\mathrm{span}_A\langle D\rangle\le\tfrac14\cdot4c(K)=c(K)$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.8.2.** Let $c(K)$ be the crossing number of a knot $K$ and $V_K$ its Jones polynomial. You may use: $c(K)\ge\mathrm{span}\,V_K$ for every knot; a reduced alternating diagram with $n$ crossings has $\mathrm{span}\langle D\rangle=4n$; every alternating knot has a reduced alternating diagram. Let $K$ be an alternating knot. Show that $c(K)=\mathrm{span}\,V_K$.
answer: Squeeze: $\mathrm{span}\,V_K\le c(K)\le n=\mathrm{span}\,V_K$.

solutions.title: Squeeze
solutions.body: Let $D$ be a reduced alternating diagram of $K$ with $n$ crossings. By definition $c(K)\le n$. By the span formula, $\mathrm{span}\langle D\rangle=4n$, hence $\mathrm{span}\,V_K=\tfrac14\mathrm{span}\langle D\rangle=n$. By 4.8.1, $\mathrm{span}\,V_K\le c(K)$. So $n=\mathrm{span}\,V_K\le c(K)\le n$, and $c(K)=n=\mathrm{span}\,V_K$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.8.3.** Use that for an alternating knot with a reduced alternating diagram with $n$ crossings, $c(K)=n$. Determine the crossing number $c(K)$ of the knot $K$ depicted by the diagram $D$ in the picture (Figure 4.7), which is reduced and alternating. Justify your answer.

solutions.title: Count crossings
solutions.body:
Counting the breaks in the under-strands (equivalently, the separate arcs of the drawing) shows that $D$ has $n=11$ crossings; $D$ is reduced and alternating (as given). By Problem 4.7.3, $\mathrm{span}\langle D\rangle=4\cdot11$, so $\mathrm{span}\,V_K=11$. By Problems 4.8.1–4.8.2, $11=\mathrm{span}\,V_K\le c(K)\le11$.

**Answer: $c(K)=11$.**
